newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: MRTA rebel's wife warns of risk to jailed comrades.
newsitem.headline: MRTA rebel's wife warns of risk to jailed comrades.

text.p: The wife of a jailed leader of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) on Saturday warned that Peruvian authorities could take revenge on her husband and other political prisoners for the rebel takeover of the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima.

Neli Gutierrez fled to Chile after her husband Miguel Rincon, one of the guerrilla group's national directorate, was captured along with American Lori Berenson when police raided an MRTA safe house in Lima a year ago.

In a phone interview with Colombia's AM-PM TV news programme, Gutierrez called on the MRTA commando, holed up in the diplomatic residence with about 340 hostages, to consider the consequences for their imprisoned comrades if their dramatic operation went wrong.
"I ask the MRTA commando to think about everybody and the best outcome for their future. If the MRTA begins to kill hostages, what will come next?" Gutierrez said.
"The Peruvian government has never respected the rights of Miguel and other political prisoners. Any violent actions by the MRTA (in the residence) could lead to reprisals," she added.

One of the rebel group's central demands since it stormed the embassy residence on Tuesday night in the middle of an elegant party has been that President Alberto Fujimori should free about 400 imprisoned MRTA insurgents.
As indications grow that hardliner Fujimori may be contemplating a military strike to dislodge the rebels from the building, Gutierrez said more violence would lead nowhere.
"Fujimori should take a direct role in dialogue with the MRTA. Peru has been living under Fujimori's extreme authoritarianism and now he can see that this doesn't lead anywhere," she told AM-PM.

Rincon is being held in Yanamayo jail -- which boasts some of the toughest conditions of all Peru's prisons. It was built at an altitude of more than 13,000 feet (4,000 meters) near the town of Puno on Peru's southern high plains, where temperatures regularly plunge below freezing.

Berenson was also being held there but both are kept in tiny, locked cells for 23-1/2 hours a day and have no contact. Rincon and Berenson were convicted by a secret military tribunal on charges of plotting an MRTA strike on Congress.

"These prisoners have virtually no contact with the outside world. Any correspondence is totally censored and family members are often not allowed direct contact. Their rights are being totally violated," Gutierrez, who runs a human rights group in Santiago, said.
